what_its_for: Aprepitant helps prevent nausea and vomiting caused by chemotherapy (cancer treatment) or surgery. It works by blocking signals in your brain that trigger the urge to vomit. It is usually used together with other anti-nausea medicines for best results.
how_to_take: Swallow the capsule whole with a full glass of water. You can take it with or without food. For chemotherapy-related nausea, take your first dose about 1 hour before your chemotherapy treatment begins. Continue taking it on the days that follow as directed by your doctor. Do not open, crush, or chew the capsule.
dosing: The usual dose for chemotherapy nausea is: Day 1 – take one 125 mg capsule about 1 hour before chemotherapy. Day 2 and Day 3 – take one 80 mg capsule each morning. For surgery-related nausea, a single 40 mg dose is taken within 3 hours before going under anesthesia. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions, as your dose may be different.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. Call your doctor or pharmacist if you are unsure what to do.
storage: Store aprepitant at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it in the original packaging and away from heat, light, and moisture. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not store it in the bathroom. Dispose of any unused or expired medicine safely by following your local pharmacy or community take-back guidelines.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking large amounts of grapefruit juice while taking this medicine, as it may increase the level of aprepitant in your blood and cause unwanted side effects. Tell your doctor about ALL medicines, vitamins, and herbal supplements you take, because aprepitant can interact with many drugs, including blood thinners like warfarin, certain steroids, birth control pills, and other medicines. Birth control pills may be less effective while you are taking aprepitant and for 28 days after your last dose — use a backup form of contraception such as condoms during this time.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away if you experience: a severe allergic reaction (hives, rash, swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat, or difficulty breathing); severe skin reactions; unusual bruising or bleeding (especially if you take blood thinners); signs of liver problems such as yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe stomach pain; or if your nausea and vomiting are not controlled. Also tell your doctor if you develop any new or worsening symptoms.
when_it_works: Aprepitant starts working before your chemotherapy begins because you take it 1 hour in advance. It helps prevent nausea and vomiting during the first 24 hours after chemotherapy (called acute nausea) as well as nausea that can develop 2 to 5 days later (called delayed nausea). Most people notice better control of nausea throughout their treatment cycle when this medicine is used as directed.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. The safety of aprepitant during pregnancy is not fully known. Because this medicine may make hormonal birth control less effective, use an additional backup method of contraception during treatment and for 28 days after your last dose. Elderly patients: Older adults can generally take this medicine safely, but your doctor will monitor you closely. Liver problems: If you have severe liver disease, your doctor may need to adjust your treatment. Children: Aprepitant is approved for use in children for certain types of chemotherapy nausea — your child's doctor will determine the correct dose based on weight.
